title: A bigger harvest estimate than expected (fictional)
setup: A fictional agriculture office in fictional Westmark publishes its harvest estimate for a grain. The estimate comes in above what forecasters expected and above last year. At the same time, a fictional neighbouring region is in a dry spell, and its crop is still in the fields. All places, offices and figures are fictional.
pricedIn: Good weather all summer had led many traders to expect a large crop, and the simulated grain price had drifted lower for weeks. Some private estimates were even higher than the official consensus.
question: Surprise = 126.0 − 120.0 = +6.0 million tonnes, a bigger crop than expected. Which reactions are plausible?

reactions.text: Price falls, as more supply is coming than expected.
reactions.explanation: A bigger crop is more supply. That tends to weigh on price, as a tendency only.

reactions.text: Price hardly moves, or even rises, because the big crop was already priced in.
reactions.explanation: The price had already fallen for weeks and some estimates were higher still. Traders who sold early may buy back after the report.

reactions.text: Price rises because the dry spell next door takes over the story.
reactions.explanation: Supply is about the whole market. Worry about the neighbouring crop could outweigh good news at home.

reactions.text: Price must fall exactly 5%, since the crop is 5% above the consensus.
reactions.explanation: 6.0 ÷ 120.0 = 5%, but price does not move one-for-one with a surprise. There is no fixed formula for the reaction.

takeaway: A bigger-than-expected harvest points to more supply, but what was priced in and what is happening elsewhere can lead to very different reactions. Seasonal reports are scenarios, not forecasts.
